start.staff: Open the course, pick a band, and read the first step with your class. The teacher note for the intro is above.

nq.title: Number Quest: math lessons for grades {grades}, mapped to CCSS-M
nq.description: Number Quest is a free math course for grades {grades}: {steps} short steps through the Numberworks, played through {gameList}, with every step mapped to the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics. One step (Explorer 7.3, chance language) is flagged enrichment and maps to no standard, and the map says so.
nq.h1: Number Quest: math with a map you can show anyone
nq.lead: A winding path through Netville's Numberworks with Tally the cat, on three streets. The Launchpad gardens, for kindergarten to grade 2: counting, joining, tens and ones, the equals sign, hundreds, shapes and measuring, with the Garden Gate at the end. The Explorer street, for grades 3 to 5: place value, joining and splitting, groups and shares, fractions at the Bakery, measuring at the Measure Shop, shapes at the Building Yard, data at the Fairground, and the Vault of Measures at the street's end. The Pro towers, for grades 6 to 8: ratios and rates, negative numbers, expressions and equations, proportion and scale, slope and lines, geometry and the Pythagorean theorem, and data and chance, with the Great Clock at the end. Students read a short deck, pass a three-question check, play the game mission, and earn Tally Marks and mastery laps as they go. No hearts, no timers that punish, no leaderboards: mistakes are part of the lesson, and the Jumble is there to make them.

badges.units: {streets, plural, one {One street} other {# streets}} · {units} units

promise.li1: One town all the way through: the Numberworks, where every number has a job to do, Tally the cat counting at your side, and the Jumble mixing numbers up so students learn to spot how. The Launchpad gardens lead on to the Explorer street and the Explorer street to the Pro towers, and a learner can move between them at any time.
promise.li2: Every worked example opens with an estimate: the course's “Rough first” habit, so checking whether an answer is the right size becomes reflex.
promise.li3: Short reading decks, then a three-question check, then the game mission itself. A step counts as finished only when the mission is actually completed, not just opened.
promise.li4: Tally Marks for doing, never for being first or fastest: checks passed, missions completed, mastery laps and reviews all earn them, and they are never spent or ranked.
promise.li5: Mastery laps, honestly labeled: finishing a unit records its Lap 1, and the unit's ring fills. Laps 2 (the same steps with bigger numbers) and 3 (a mixed circuit with a boss round) are designed but still being built, and the course says so wherever they are named, rather than pretending a replay is new content.
promise.li6: The full standards map on this page: every step's primary CCSS-M statements, the statements it also covers, and the ones it builds toward, labeled as preparation and never counted as coverage.

crew.p: Seven were built for the Launchpad gardens, one for each unit, from Garden Count to Kitchen Rush: every instruction in them is read aloud, so a child can play before they can read well. On the Explorer street, three are quiz, race and fluency engines the school may already know from the open library; the fourth, Fraction Factory, was built for this course and is where Tally makes her home. The Fairground borrows a fifth: Data Detective from CS Quest for its data cases. Seven more were built for the Pro towers, one for each unit, from Lantern Mix to Launch Lab: each round is planned first and then run, a wrong plan is shown as it really turns out, and every line is read aloud unless the student turns the voice off.
crew.gardenCount: Launchpad Unit 1, The Counting Patch (kindergarten). Count apples in a sunny garden: pick the number your helper asks for (step 1.1), find the bed with more or fewer (1.2), and build teen numbers on a ten-frame (1.3). Each chapter is six rounds, and the sixth right round completes the mission.
crew.lilyHop: Launchpad Unit 2, The Joining Pond (kindergarten to grade 1). Frogs hop together and hop away within 10 (step 2.1), a number is split into its partners and made up to 10 (2.2), and a row of numbered lily pads carries adding and taking away to 20 (2.3). Every round is answered by hopping to one of three pads.
crew.crateStacker: Launchpad Unit 3, The Tens Trellis (grade 1). A crate is a one and a tower of ten crates is a ten: build and read two-digit numbers (step 3.1), say which truck has more and pick the sign (3.2), and add tens and ones with totals under 100 (3.3).
crew.balanceBridge: Launchpad Unit 4, The Balance Bridge (grades 1 and 2). A see-saw drawbridge goes level only when both sides weigh the same: true or not true and the missing number (step 4.1), spoken stories the blocks act out (4.2), and odd, even and equal rows (4.3). A wrong number is tried on the bridge, so the child sees it lean and tries again.
crew.rocketSupply: Launchpad Unit 5, The Hundreds Hedge (grade 2). A pallet is a hundred, a rack is a ten and a canister is a one: load and read three-digit numbers (step 5.1), skip count and compare along the fuel gauge (5.2), and add and subtract within 100 with the regrouping shown on the pad (5.3).
crew.shapeHunt: Launchpad Unit 6, The Shape Shed (kindergarten to grade 2). A tidy-up treasure hunt in a cosy house: find a shape whatever its size or the way it is turned (step 6.1), build a bigger shape from the right pieces (6.2), and share pizzas, pies and cakes into halves, fourths and thirds (6.3).
crew.kitchenRush: Launchpad Unit 7, The Measuring Meadow (kindergarten to grade 2). Measure in cubes and on a ruler (step 7.1), read clocks and count coins (7.2), sort and read graphs (7.3). Its fourth chapter is the Garden Gate (7.4), the street's finale: a mixed review of all seven units. Nothing in it is timed; the rush is in the name only.
crew.brainBoard: A category quiz board, played solo as a practice board. In Number Quest it is the fluency mission for steps 1.1 and 2.3 and for the Measure Shop and Building Yard boards of Units 5 and 6 (measures, money, perimeter and area, lines and grids): the step's own deck and check teach the skill, and scoring 3,000 points on the board is what completes the mission, and the board saves as the student plays, so a lesson can span sittings.
crew.sumRacer: An arithmetic kart racer. Its Number Quest missions are locked to the taught skill: a Rounding Run track built for step 1.2, addition-only and subtraction-only Trading Post races with 3- and 4-digit trades in Unit 2, and the all-tables, sharing and mixed Grand Prix tracks of Unit 3. The game opens on the step's track and stays there, so the win that completes the mission is a win at that skill.
crew.questRace: An island race, played solo as a practice race against three island racers. In Number Quest it carries steps 1.3 (patterns), 5.2 (timetables) and the finale 7.4, the Vault Run: the deck and check teach the skill, and finishing the whole race, all the way to the podium, is what completes it.
crew.dataDetective: CS Quest's data cases, borrowed for the Fairground: sort a messy table, chart it, and spot the claim the data does not support. In Number Quest it carries steps 7.1 (Chart It) and 7.2 (My Data, the student's own class survey), with its cases untouched.
crew.lanternMix: Pro Unit 1, The Mixing Tower (grade 6). Lanterns glow by the ratio of two oils: match a glow with an equal ratio (step 1.1), set a tank from a unit rate (1.2), and fill to a percent or change units along a lit path (1.3). A match is decided by the ratio, never by color alone.
crew.subZero: Pro Unit 2, The Cold Store (grades 6 and 7). A night-time lab with a thermometer that goes below zero: pour a pot into jars to divide by a fraction (step 2.1), place and compare readings and their distance from zero (2.2), and plan changes that add, subtract, multiply and divide with negatives (2.3).
crew.machineLine: Pro Unit 3, The Machine Hall (grades 6 and 7). A line of machines does one thing each to a number: build the line for an expression and run it (step 3.1), say whether two lines always give the same output (3.2), and run a line backward to solve an equation or an inequality (3.3).
crew.scaleScout: Pro Unit 4, The Map Room (grade 7). A surveyor's map on a board: find which walker's distance is proportional to the time and its constant (step 4.1), turn map centimeters into real meters and back (4.2), and work out percent change and percent error (4.3). Nothing in it is priced.
crew.skyLines: Pro Unit 5, The Sky Wires (grade 8). Zip wires between floating islands on a coordinate grid: set a wire's steepness from rise and run (step 5.1), write it as y = mx + b from a table, a story or a graph (5.2), and find where two wires meet, or show they never do (5.3).
crew.keepBuilder: Pro Unit 6, The Drafting Keep (grades 6 to 8). A castle builder's plan: fill rooms with crates and cover towers from their nets (step 6.1), find angles and move stones by a slide, flip, turn or resize (6.2), and size ladders and spans with the Pythagorean theorem (6.3).
crew.launchLab: Pro Unit 7, The Test Range (grades 6 to 8). A launcher on a test range makes the data: read center and spread from dot and box plots (step 7.1), predict from a chance model and compare with a run (7.2), and compare two data sets and use a trend line (7.3). Its fourth chapter is the Great Clock (7.4), the street's finale: one multi-step problem for each of the seven units.
crew.fractionFactory: Tally's Bakery production line: cut wholes into fair shares, re-slice to make sizes match, and add slices for real orders. The whole of Unit 4, and the course's flagship Jumble beat: adding the bottoms too.

units.h: The streets, their units and their steps
units.p: {steps} steps on {streets, plural, one {one street} other {# streets}}, in order, each ending in its game mission or its classroom talk. A unit's stone is planted when its steps are done. Each street ends inside its Unit 7, at a finale: the Garden Gate on Launchpad, the Vault of Measures on Explorer and the Great Clock on Pro.

map.p: Every step, mapped. “Primary” is what the step teaches and its check assesses. “Also covers” is practiced inside the step but taught as primary elsewhere. “Builds toward” is preparation only: the course names it so you can see the road ahead, and never counts it as coverage. The practice named is the step's Mathematical Practice spotlight.
map.codes: locked CCSS-M statements, every unit and finale shown
map.lock: This map publishes the Phase 0 standards lock (2026-11-04) and the Phase 2 lock (2026-11-05), the Explorer Units 1–7 and finale statement codes; the Launchpad lock (unit by unit, 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13), the Launchpad Units 1–7 and finale statement codes; and the Pro lock (2026-11-14), the Pro Units 1–7 and finale statement codes, all verified against the published Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (NGA Center & CCSSO, 2010). Explorer step 7.3 cites no code anywhere: chance language has no CCSS home before grade 6, so it is published as enrichment, plainly flagged. Pro is the major work of grades 6–8, not every statement: the list below the map names what it does not cover.

notes.p: One short note per unit, written to print: the habit to open with and the trap to watch for. The same notes print with the standards map.

safety.li1: No hearts and no mistake tax: a wrong answer names the mix-up kindly and the student tries again, free, as many times as they need.
safety.li2: No leaderboards and no ranking between children. Tally Marks are a personal total to watch grow; they buy nothing and are never spent.
safety.li3: The daily goal is the student's own choice of 1, 2 or 3 activities, and missing it costs nothing: there is no streak to break.
safety.li4: The course collects nothing new. Progress, checks and marks use the same kid-safe machinery as the rest of Oomba Academy: no chat, no ads, no third parties.

print.p: The standards map and the teacher notes are the printed pack for this course: one map to file with your planning, and one short note per unit to read before the lesson. They print on their own page, without the site around them.

faq.q1: Do I need to be a math specialist?
faq.a1: No. Each step teaches its own idea in plain words before the game, and the teacher note for the unit tells you the habit to open with and the trap to watch for.
faq.q2: Which standards does it teach?
faq.a2: The Common Core State Standards for Mathematics for kindergarten to grade 8: the Launchpad street covers kindergarten to grade 2, the Explorer street grades 3 to 5, and the Pro street the major work of grades 6 to 8 (circles, cylinders, cones and spheres, exponents and scientific notation, and irrational numbers are not in it, and this page lists every statement it leaves out). Every step lists its primary statements on this page, with the statements it also covers and the ones it builds toward kept separate and labeled. One step lists none: Explorer 7.3 teaches chance language, which has no standard before grade 6, and it is flagged as enrichment so no one mistakes it for coverage.
faq.q3: How long does a step take?
faq.a3: About ten minutes: a short deck, a three-question check, and one game chapter. A street is a welcome, seven units and a finale, so one street is just under four hours of lessons; the course has {steps} steps in all, and mastery laps stretch it much further for students who finish early.
faq.q4: What are Tally Marks and laps?
faq.a4: Tally Marks are points for doing: a passed check, a finished mission, a completed lap. They are never spent and never ranked. Finishing a unit records Lap 1 of its mastery laps. Laps 2 (bigger numbers) and 3 (a mixed circuit with a boss round) are designed but still being built; the course labels them as such until they can really be played.
faq.a5: Yes: free for classrooms, with no ads and nothing to install. It runs in the browser on any device, including Chromebooks.

start.p: Open the course and walk the first step with your class. Kindergarten to grade 2 starts on the Launchpad street, grades 3 to 5 on the Explorer street and grades 6 to 8 on the Pro street; Tally's Sorting Game can choose for a learner who is not sure. The teacher notes for every welcome are above.

The teacher notes for every welcome are above.

classroom.lead: Connect your Google Classroom in a few clicks. At first Oomba Academy can only see your classes and their students. It posts nothing until you allow posting.
classroom.li1: Import your roster in one click, and it refreshes itself every 6 hours. Students are matched by their Google account.
classroom.li2: Post a lesson as a Classroom assignment, with its link and due date, or share it as a material.
classroom.li3: Completion grades flow back to Classroom: each student’s grade out of 100 is the share of the lesson’s steps they finished, not how many answers were right. Send them yourself, or turn on automatic grades.
classroom.li4: Post to the class stream when a live game starts or a lesson is ready, in your own words.
classroom.li5: Oomba Academy doesn’t ask Classroom for student emails, and never sends Google a student’s name, answers or games.
classroom.note: Assignments, materials, grades and announcements work once you allow posting, a separate step. Each teacher connects their own Google account, and your school’s Google admin may need to allow Oomba Academy first.

games.sumRacer: Math facts from adding to 10 up to times tables and division, as a kart race. Two players can race on one screen.
games.wordHunt: Themed word searches with words read aloud, a daily puzzle and a race-a-friend mode.
games.sharkPlank: Hangman for early readers, with every word read aloud.
games.wordPeek: A daily word puzzle with clues after every guess, plus 4- and 6-letter versions.
games.castleClash: Real chess, with short lessons for every piece, 24 checkmate puzzles and a robot at four levels.
games.connectFour: Four in a row against a friend or a robot: plan ahead and block the other player.
games.brickDrop: Falling-block puzzles: see where each shape fits and clear whole rows.
games.loopLab: Make beats with drums, bass and melody, chain them into a song and clear 10 music challenges.
games.beatLanes: Tap in time to nine songs, from Twinkle Twinkle to the Can-Can.
games.swishFlick: Flick to shoot hoops: the direction aims the ball and the speed sets how far it flies.
games.munchMaze: A maze chase: plan a route, collect every dot and dodge the Gloops.
games.heroOfSunvale: A big 3D adventure: explore a kingdom, help the villagers on missions and win friendly battles to free the princess.
games.roboRoute: Guide a robot with blocks: sequences, loops, conditionals, variables and functions, then fix the bugs.
games.dataDetective: Sort, chart and clean data, then make claims the evidence supports.
games.packetPost: Send packets across a network, pick strong passphrases and spot online tricks.
games.insideTheMachine: Build and fix computers: parts, inputs and outputs, bits and pixels, designing for everyone.
games.tugOfMath: Math questions picked for each grade from 1 to 8, from adding within 20 to equations, as a tug of war. Play the computer or a friend on one screen.
games.doodleHoot: Draw a word for the others, or guess theirs as they draw: type it, say it, or use letter tiles. Easy, Medium or Tricky words in 13 languages, live with family and friends or on one device.
games.remisQuietMeadow: A classroom noise meter: keep the room calm so Remi the red panda can nap, and count up the quiet time together.
games.quietBounce: A classroom noise meter: a box of bouncy balls rests while the room is calm, then jiggles, rattles and jumps when it gets too loud.
games.popcornHush: A classroom noise meter: keep the room calm so the popcorn stays unpopped, because too much noise makes the kernels pop.
games.sudoku: Logic puzzles from a tiny 4×4 with pictures to the classic 9×9: every row, column and box gets each number once.
games.sumSpotter: Spot the number that two others add up to (or multiply to make), from sums to 10 to times tables, with a 60-second Rush.
games.wordTrail: The sight words, from Pre-primer to Grade 3, on a storybook trail with Bramble the hedgehog: hear a word and tap it, finish a sentence, spell it with letter tiles, in short lessons with a daily streak.
games.crossword: Turn any vocabulary list into a crossword: type or upload the words, add clues or let AI write them, and share it with the class.
games.mistakeHunt: Find and fix the mistakes in a short passage: teachers paste their own text, plant spelling, grammar and punctuation mistakes, then share, assign or print it.
games.typingPets: Learn to type one key at a time, with colors for each finger: 40 short lessons from the home row to numbers and symbols, timed tests, and an egg to crack with a new pet after every lesson.

math.name: Math games
math.short: Addition, subtraction, multiplication (times tables) and division
math.title: Free math games: addition, subtraction, multiplication
math.description: Practice addition, subtraction, multiplication and division facts in Sum Racer, a free math racing game for grades 1 to 5, with two-player races.
math.lead: Sum Racer is a free math facts game: every right answer speeds a kart past the other racers. Pick the track that matches what your class is learning, from addition to 10 up to the times tables and division, and run a quick race at the start of a lesson. It works in the browser, on Chromebooks, tablets and the classroom board.

tracks.h: Seven tracks: addition and subtraction to 100, multiplication (times tables) to 12, division
tracks.li5: Multiplication: all the times tables up to 12
tracks.p: Students can also pick exactly which times tables to practice.

math.tips: Start a lesson with a five-minute race on the track you are working on, or put two students on one device for a head-to-head race.

faq.q1: What math does Sum Racer cover?
faq.a1: Addition to 10, addition and subtraction to 20 and 100, the times tables up to 12, division facts, and a mixed track with all four operations.
faq.q2: Can two students race each other?
faq.a2: Yes. Two players can race on one screen.
faq.a3: Yes. It is free to play, with no ads, and students can start without signing up.
faq.q4: Can my child practice just one times table at home?
faq.a4: Yes. In Sum Racer they can pick exactly which times tables to practice.

math.home: A five-minute race after school keeps math facts fresh. Pick the track your child is working on at school, or choose exactly which times tables to practice, and race each other on the same screen.

words.name: Reading and spelling games
words.short: Word searches, hangman and a daily word puzzle
words.title: Free reading and spelling games for kids
words.description: Word searches, hangman and a daily word puzzle for ages 5 to 14, with words read aloud for early readers. Free, no ads, in any browser.
words.h1: Reading and spelling games for early and growing readers
words.lead: Three word games that build spelling and vocabulary. Shark Plank and Word Hunt read words aloud, so they suit early readers. Word Peek is a daily word puzzle for confident spellers.
words.tips: Use a Word Hunt theme as a warm-up for a topic, solve the Daily Peek together on the board and talk about each guess, or set Shark Plank for early finishers.

faq.q1: Do the games read words aloud?
faq.a1: Shark Plank reads each word aloud, and in Word Hunt students can tap any word to hear it.
faq.q2: Is there a daily puzzle?
faq.a2: Yes. Word Hunt and Word Peek each have a new daily puzzle, and in Word Peek a student can set a secret word for a friend.
faq.q3: Can I use my own spelling list?
faq.a3: Not in these games yet. You can describe a spelling game with your words to the Builder, and it will make one for your class.
faq.q4: Which word game suits my child’s reading level?
faq.a4: Shark Plank and Word Hunt read words aloud, so they suit kids who are still building their reading. Word Peek is for confident spellers.

words.home: Make the Daily Peek a family habit at breakfast and talk about each guess, or let a younger reader play Shark Plank with the sound on, so every word is read aloud.

strategy.name: Chess and strategy games
strategy.short: Chess lessons and puzzles, four in a row, block puzzles
strategy.title: Free chess and strategy games for kids
strategy.description: Learn chess with short lessons and puzzles, then play a friend or a robot. Plus four in a row and falling-block puzzles, free for ages 5 to 14.
strategy.h1: Chess and strategy games that build thinking skills
strategy.lead: Strategy games ask students to plan ahead, spot patterns and think about what the other player will do. Castle Clash teaches chess from the first move. Drop Four and Brick Drop are quick games of planning and patterns.
strategy.tips: Run a class chess club with Castle Clash's lessons and puzzles, or pair students on one device for a game of Drop Four.

faq.q1: Can kids learn chess from scratch?
faq.a1: Yes. Castle Clash has a short lesson for every piece and 24 checkmate puzzles, then a robot to play at four levels.
faq.q2: Can two students play on one device?
faq.a2: Yes. Castle Clash and Drop Four both have a two-player mode on one screen.
faq.a3: Castle Clash's robot has four levels, and Drop Four's robot has Easy, Normal and Hard.
faq.q4: Can I learn chess alongside my child?
faq.a4: Yes. Castle Clash’s lessons start with how each piece moves, so a grown-up who has never played can learn too, then play their child on the same screen.

strategy.home: Learn chess together: do one Castle Clash lesson a day, then play each other on one screen. Drop Four fits into any spare five minutes.

music.name: Music games
music.short: Make beats and play along to songs
music.title: Music games for kids: make beats and play in rhythm
music.description: Make your own beats in Loop Lab and tap along to nine songs in Beat Lanes. Free music games for ages 5 to 14, with no ads, in any browser.
music.h1: Music games: make beats and play along
music.lead: Loop Lab is a beat maker: students tap squares to build a loop of drums, bass and melody and hear it straight away. Beat Lanes is a rhythm game with nine songs, from Twinkle Twinkle to the Can-Can.
music.tips: Use Loop Lab's music challenges to explore patterns and repetition, or play a Beat Lanes song as a quick brain break. Headphones help in a busy room.

faq.q1: Do students need to read music?
faq.a1: No. Both games use colors and timing, not written notes.
faq.q2: Can students make whole songs?
faq.a2: Yes. In Loop Lab they can chain patterns into a song and play it back like a little concert.
faq.q3: Does my child need an instrument or music lessons?
faq.a3: No. Everything happens in the browser, with colors and timing instead of written notes.

music.home: Loop Lab needs no lessons and no instrument: kids make a beat, chain it into a song and play it back to the family. Headphones help in a busy house.

brainBreaks.name: Brain break games
brainBreaks.short: Quick games for a short break
brainBreaks.title: Quick brain break games for the classroom
brainBreaks.description: Short, fun games for a 3 to 5 minute classroom brain break: rhythm, hoops, mazes, falling blocks and a daily word puzzle. Free, no ads, no sign-up.
brainBreaks.h1: Quick brain break games for the classroom
brainBreaks.lead: A few minutes of play between lessons helps students reset. These games start in seconds, need no sign-up, and are easy to stop when the timer ends.
brainBreaks.tips: Set a timer for 3 to 5 minutes, put a game on the board and let the class take turns, or let students play on their own devices.

faq.q1: How long should a brain break be?
faq.a1: Many teachers use 3 to 5 minutes. These games have short rounds, so it is easy to stop on time.
faq.q2: Can the whole class play on one screen?
faq.a2: Yes. Put a game on the board and take turns. Beat Lanes and Swish Flick work well with the class cheering along.

makeAGame.name: Make your own game
makeAGame.short: Kids design games with the AI Builder
makeAGame.title: Make your own video game: AI game maker for kids
makeAGame.description: Kids describe a game in plain words and the Builder makes it, showing its steps. No coding needed, ad-free, for ages 5 to 14, and private until shared.
makeAGame.h1: Make your own game, no coding needed
makeAGame.lead: On Oomba Academy, students describe the game they want and the AI Builder makes it. Then they play it, test it and ask for changes, one idea at a time.

how.li1: Describe: type an idea, like “a maze where a cat collects fish”, and add a drawing or photo if you like.
how.li2: Build: the Builder makes the game and shows its steps behind the scenes while it works.
how.li3: Play and test: try it out and notice what to change.
how.li4: Improve: ask for changes in plain words, one at a time.

skills.p: Planning an idea, writing clear instructions, testing, finding and fixing problems, and improving a design step by step: the habits of programmers and game designers.

safe.p: The Builder follows fixed kid-safety rules: no gore, no gambling, no real brands or real people, no chat or data collection inside games, and no links out. Every game runs in a locked sandbox.

makeAGame.tips: Add a “build a game” step to a lesson with the idea students start from. A project that works well: each student designs a review game for the topic you are teaching, then classmates play it and give feedback.

faq.q1: Do students need to know how to code?
faq.a1: No. They describe the game in their own words. The Builder shows its steps as it works, so curious students can see how a game is put together.
faq.q2: Who can see the games students make?
faq.a2: Only the student, until they share it. They can share it with friends or their class, and a game for everyone is reviewed before anyone else can play it.
faq.q4: My child wants to make video games. Where do they start?
faq.a4: With a small idea, like a maze or a catching game. They describe it, play it, then ask for one change at a time. Later, many kids also try coding tools like Scratch.
faq.a5: Not exactly. The Builder writes the code. Your child does the design, the testing and the explaining, which are big parts of making games, and the steps it shows let curious kids see how a game is put together.
faq.a6: Nothing. Every player with an account (just a made-up name and a password) gets free Builder messages each day.

parents.h: For parents: why making beats only playing
parents.p1: Making a game is active screen time. Your child plans an idea, explains it clearly, tests what the Builder made and decides what to fix next: the same steps game designers use.
parents.p2: It makes a good weekend project to do together, and building is free every day.

ideas.li1: A maze where a cat collects fish
ideas.li2: A quiz about my favorite animals
ideas.li3: A space game where you catch falling stars
ideas.li5: A puzzle where you sort colors into jars
ideas.p: Then ask for one change at a time, like “make the cat faster” or “add a second level”.

scratch.h: Where it fits next to Scratch and coding
scratch.p: Scratch and Code.org teach coding with blocks. The Builder is different: kids design in words, and the Builder writes the game while showing its steps. Many kids do both, and the Builder can be a first step before code.

cs.title: Computer science games for kids: code, data and networks
cs.description: Four free computer science games for grades 3 to 8: block coding in Robo Route, data in Data Detective, networks in Packet Post and hardware in Inside the Machine.

a8.name: Ages 8 and 9
a8.short: Times tables, spelling, first chess games and music
a8.title: Free learning games for 8 and 9 year olds
a8.description: Free, ad-free browser games for 8 and 9 year olds: times tables, spelling, first chess moves and music. No downloads and no chat with strangers.
a8.h1: Learning games for 8 and 9 year olds
a8.lead: At 8 and 9, kids are learning their times tables, reading longer words and loving games they can win. These games keep rounds short, read words aloud where it helps, and let two kids play on one screen.

fit.sumRacer: Start with adding to 10 or 20, then move on to the 2, 5 and 10 times tables when they’re ready.
fit.wordHunt: Themed word searches for growing readers: they can tap any word to hear it read aloud.
fit.sharkPlank: Good for kids still building their reading: every word is read aloud.
fit.castleClash: A short lesson for each piece, then the robot at its easiest level, so a first chess game isn’t a wall of rules.
fit.connectFour: Quick games about planning ahead, against a sibling or the robot on Easy.
fit.loopLab: Tap squares to make a beat and hear it loop right away. No need to read music.
fit.beatLanes: Tap in time to songs they know, starting with Twinkle Twinkle.
fit.munchMaze: A maze chase with an Easy mode: plan a route and collect every dot.
fit.tugOfMath: Pick grade 2 or 3: adding, taking away and times tables, with the computer on Easy until they win it.
fit.doodleHoot: Picture words to guess and spell: spelling practice that feels like a party game.

faq.q2: Are the games too hard for an 8 year old?
faq.a2: Each one starts easy. Sum Racer begins with adding to 10, Castle Clash’s robot has an easy level, and Shark Plank reads every word aloud.
faq.q3: Can two kids play on one device?
faq.a3: Yes. Sum Racer, Castle Clash and Drop Four have a two-player mode on one screen.
faq.q4: Can an 8 year old use the AI Builder?

a10.name: Ages 10 and 11
a10.short: Times tables and division, word and chess puzzles, making games
a10.title: Free learning games for 10 and 11 year olds
a10.description: Free, ad-free browser games for 10 and 11 year olds: times tables and division, a daily word puzzle, chess puzzles, music, and making their own games.
a10.h1: Learning games for 10 and 11 year olds
a10.lead: At 10 and 11, kids want a real challenge and a say in what they play. These games go up to all the times tables and division, chess puzzles and a daily word puzzle, and the Builder lets them make a game of their own.
a10.abcya: Outgrowing ABCya? Its games are for PreK to grade 6. Oomba Academy is made for ages 5 to 14.

make.p: Kids this age love making their own games. They describe one in plain words, like “a quiz about volcanoes” or “a maze with a robot”, and the Builder makes it. Then they test it and ask for changes. It’s free every day.

fit.sumRacer: Ready for the harder facts: all the times tables up to 12, division, and a mixed track with all four operations.
fit.wordPeek: A daily puzzle that rewards careful thinking, with a clue after every guess, just as their vocabulary takes off.
fit.castleClash: Past the basics? 24 checkmate puzzles and harder robot levels give them something real to beat.
fit.brickDrop: Speed builds quickly, which suits kids who want a real challenge and like beating their own best.
fit.loopLab: Old enough to plan a whole song: chain beats together and clear the 10 music challenges.
fit.heroOfSunvale: Bigger than a quick game: missions to read and follow, and a 3D kingdom to explore at their own pace.
fit.swishFlick: A quick break with a bit of physics: the direction of the flick aims the ball and its speed sets how far it flies.
fit.tugOfMath: Grades 4 and 5 bring bigger times and order of operations; two players can tug on one tablet or smartboard.
fit.doodleHoot: Tricky words and two-word answers, and a race to spell them first.

faq.q2: Are the games too easy for a 10 year old?
faq.a2: No. Sum Racer goes up to all the times tables and division, Castle Clash has 24 checkmate puzzles, and Word Peek is a real daily challenge.
faq.q3: Can my child play with a sibling or a friend?
faq.a3: Yes. Sum Racer and Castle Clash have a two-player mode on one screen, and Word Hunt has a pass-the-phone race.
faq.q4: Is the AI Builder safe for an 11 year old?
faq.a4: The Builder only makes games, and it follows fixed kid-safety rules, such as no gore, no gambling, no real brands and no links out. See every rule it follows. Games stay private until your child shares them.

make.p: Describe a game in plain words and the Builder makes it: a platformer, a quiz for a school topic, a puzzle for a friend. Then test it, find what’s wrong and ask for changes. It’s free every day.

fit.castleClash: Real chess with no kiddie mode: checkmate puzzles and the robot’s hardest level are a real test, even for adults.
fit.wordPeek: Harder than the daily puzzle: Big Peek with 6 letters, or set a secret word for a friend to crack.
fit.brickDrop: Race to 40 lines in Sprint, or keep going in Marathon as it gets faster.
fit.loopLab: Teens into music can build whole songs from drums, bass and melody, not just simple beats.
fit.beatLanes: Nine songs and long combos for quick fingers.
fit.heroOfSunvale: A big 3D kingdom to explore, with missions and a dragon at the end.
fit.tugOfMath: Grades 6 to 8: percents, negative numbers, powers and equations, against the computer on Hard.

faq.q2: Is Oomba Academy too young for a 13 year old?
faq.a2: It’s made for ages 5 to 14. Older kids mostly come for the Builder, real chess and music making, which grow with them.

faq.a2: Some games, yes. Word Trail and Shark Plank read every word aloud, Word Hunt reads a word when you tap it, and Sum Racer and Tug of Math use numbers. Menus and instructions are written, so a grown-up nearby helps at first.

ai.name: Is the AI Builder safe?
ai.short: What the AI sees, what it never gets, and the rules it follows
ai.title: Is AI safe for kids? Our Builder, explained
ai.description: What the AI sees, what it never gets, and the rules it follows: a plain-words guide for parents of kids 5–14 using Oomba Academy’s AI game Builder.
ai.h1: Is the AI Builder safe for my child?
ai.lead: Oomba Academy’s Builder uses AI to turn your child’s idea into a game. Here is what it sees, what it never gets, the rules it follows and what we can’t promise, in plain words.

what.p1: The Builder makes games. Your child describes an idea, and it writes the game, shows its steps while it works and asks a question when it needs to know more.
what.p2: It is made for building games, not as a friend or companion to chat with about anything else.

sees.h: What the AI sees, and what it never gets
sees.li1: The messages, pictures and files your child gives the Builder go to Claude, an AI made by the company Anthropic, which writes the game.
sees.li2: Your child’s name and username are not sent with them.
sees.li3: Chats between friends and lesson answers are never sent to the AI.
sees.li4: Hidden location data is removed from photos and pictures before they are kept.
sees.li5: If your child uploads a profile photo, it is sent to Claude to be checked before anyone sees it.
sees.li6: Games your child wants to share with everyone are reviewed by Claude first.

rules.p: The Builder follows fixed kid-safety rules in every language, and a message can’t change them:
rules.li1: No blood, gore or realistic violence, and no horror or jump-scares. Cartoon slapstick is fine.
rules.li3: No real brands, and no real people as characters.
rules.li4: No chat between players and no collecting personal details inside games.
rules.li5: No links to other websites and no ads inside games.
rules.li6: No romantic or adult content, no bullying or hate, and nothing about self-harm, drugs, alcohol or vaping.
rules.li7: No copyrighted characters like Mario or Pokémon, and no real classmates, teachers or family members in games.
rules.p2: A request that breaks the rules is kindly refused, with ideas for something it can make instead.

public.p: A new game is private to your child. They can share it with friends or their class. A game for everyone is reviewed by Claude before anyone else can play it, and our team checks any it is unsure about. Every game runs in a locked sandbox that can’t reach the internet or your child’s account.

limits.p1: No filter is perfect. An AI can misunderstand a request or make a mistake, and a game could still have something that isn’t right for your child.
limits.p2: If you see something wrong, tap 🚩 Report on the game page. Enough reports hide a game until our team looks, and grown-ups can also email us at {email}.

check.h: Five questions to ask about any AI tool for kids
check.li1: What does it do? A tool that makes something (a game, a picture, a story) is different from a chatbot that talks about anything.
check.li2: What does it send, and to whom? Look for a plain list of what goes to the AI company, and whether your child’s name goes with it.
check.li3: What rules does it follow? A good tool for kids says what it refuses to make.
check.li4: Who sees what your child makes? Private until shared is safest.
check.li5: Can you report a problem? There should be an easy way, and a person who looks.

faq.q1: Does my child chat with an AI?
faq.a1: Only about the game they’re making. They describe what they want, and the Builder asks questions and explains its steps.
faq.q2: Is my child’s name sent to the AI?
faq.a2: No. Their name and username are not sent with their messages.
faq.q3: Can the AI make scary or violent games?
faq.a3: Games can have cartoon action, like a hero’s friendly battles, but the Builder refuses gore, realistic violence, horror and jump-scares. See every rule it follows.
faq.q4: Are the games my child makes public?
faq.a4: Not unless they share them. A game for everyone is reviewed before anyone else can play it.
faq.q5: Is the Builder a companion or a friend bot?
faq.a5: No. It is a tool for making games.

screen.name: Good screen time
screen.short: A checklist for choosing games and apps, and how to set limits
screen.title: Good screen time for kids: a parent’s guide
screen.description: How to tell good screen time from bad: ads, purchases, chat, data, and making vs scrolling. A checklist for parents, with what we do and don’t do.
screen.h1: Good screen time: how to choose games for kids 5–14
screen.lead: There’s no perfect number of minutes. What kids do on a screen, who they do it with and what it pushes them toward matter just as much. This checklist helps you judge any game or app, including ours.

experts.p1: The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests a family media plan instead of one number for every child: for school-age kids, consistent limits that protect sleep, schoolwork, physical activity and time together. Common Sense Media also looks at the quality of what kids watch and play, not only the minutes.
experts.p2: So we won’t give you a number of minutes here: you know your child. We can help you judge what those minutes are spent on.

check.h: A checklist for any game or app
check.li1: Ads: does it show ads, or videos that lead to more videos?
check.li2: Purchases: can your child spend money? Is there in-game money, loot boxes or “pay to win”?
check.li3: Strangers: can people your child doesn’t know send them messages?
check.li4: Data: does it ask your child for an email address, age, location or photos?
check.li5: Age fit: is it made for your child’s age, not just allowed for it?
check.li6: Making or scrolling: does your child solve, practice or make something, or mostly watch?
check.li7: Together: can you play it with them?

us.h: How Oomba Academy does on it, honestly
us.li2: Purchases: nothing for kids to buy, no loot boxes and no in-game money that costs money.
us.li3: Strangers: chat only with friends added by a code, filtered and reportable.
us.li4: Data: we never ask kids for an email address, age, address or location. Photos are optional: a profile photo or pictures for the Builder, with hidden location data removed and profile photos checked before anyone sees them.
us.li6: Making: kids can make their own games with the AI Builder.
us.li7: Together: several games have a two-player mode on one screen.
us.p: What we don’t have: time limits, activity reports or a parent dashboard. For limits, use your device’s own tools.

tools.h: Setting limits with your device’s tools
tools.p: These free tools from the device makers let you set daily limits, downtime and app rules:
tools.li1: Apple Screen Time on iPhone, iPad and Mac
tools.li2: Google Family Link on Android phones, tablets and Chromebooks
tools.li3: Microsoft Family Safety on Windows and Xbox

rules.li1: Play a new game together the first time.
rules.li2: Keep building and chatting in a shared room.
rules.li3: Agree on when, not only how long: after homework, not at bedtime.
rules.li4: Ask what they made or learned today.
rules.li5: Use the same rules for every screen in the house, grown-ups’ too.

faq.q1: How much screen time is OK for a 10 year old?
faq.a1: There is no single number. Pediatricians suggest consistent limits that leave room for sleep, school, being active and family time, and paying attention to what kids do on screens. A family media plan helps you decide.
faq.q2: Is educational screen time better than games?
faq.a2: Games can be educational. Look for ones where your child solves, practices or makes something, with no ads or purchases pulling them along.
faq.q3: Does Oomba Academy have time limits?
faq.a3: No. Use your device’s tools, like Apple Screen Time, Google Family Link or Microsoft Family Safety.
faq.q4: Is making games better than playing them?
faq.a4: Both have a place. Making a game asks kids to plan, explain clearly, test and fix, so it is an active kind of screen time.

Last, how it stays safe: a made-up name with no email, friends added only with a code, and games kept private until the child chooses to share.

research.name: The research
research.title: Does game-based learning work? What the research says
research.description: What three large research reviews found about learning games and gamification, in plain words for teachers, with effect sizes and full citations.
research.h1: Does game-based learning work? What the research says
research.lead: Three large reviews pooled the results of many studies on learning games and on game elements in lessons. Here is what they found, in plain words, and what it does not prove.

clark.h: Learning games, compared with teaching without games
clark.stat: From the 50th to about the 63rd percentile
clark.p: Across studies that compared digital learning games with teaching without games, students who learned with games did better on tests of what they learned.
clark.small: Clark, Tanner-Smith and Killingsworth (2016): learning outcomes, games compared with no games, g = 0.33.

wouters.h: Serious games, compared with conventional teaching
wouters.stat: About the 61st percentile for learning, and the 64th for remembering it later
wouters.p: Students who learned with serious games learned more than students taught in conventional ways, and they remembered more when they were tested again later.
wouters.small: Wouters, van Nimwegen, van Oostendorp and van der Spek (2013): learning d = 0.29, retention d = 0.36.

sailer.p: Adding game elements such as points, badges and leaderboards to ordinary lessons also helped what students learned.
sailer.small: Sailer and Homner (2020): gamification, cognitive learning outcomes, g = 0.49.

read.p1: A percentile says where the average student who learned with games would land among students taught without them. The 50th percentile is the middle. Moving to the 63rd percentile means the average student with games scored higher than about 63 out of 100 students taught without them.
read.p2: The small print gives each effect size (Hedges’ g or Cohen’s d): the difference between the two groups, measured in standard deviations. We turned each one into a percentile assuming normally distributed scores.

limits.li1: These are averages across many studies, ages, subjects and games. Some games helped a lot, and some did not help at all.
limits.li2: None of these studies tested Oomba Academy. They describe learning games in general, not a promise about any one game, class or student.
limits.li3: Wouters and colleagues found that serious games were not more motivating than conventional teaching, even though students learned more.
limits.li4: Gamification is not the same as a learning game: it adds game elements to ordinary lessons. We include it because points, stars and leaderboards are part of many learning games, including ours.

use.h: Using games the way the research suggests
use.p: Wouters and colleagues found that students learned more from serious games when the game was used alongside other teaching, over more than one session, and when students played in groups.
use.li1: Use a game alongside your lesson, not in place of it: a short round to practice what you just taught.
use.li2: Come back to it over several sessions instead of one long session.
use.li3: Let students play together: as a whole class, in teams, or two players on one screen.

compliance.name: Privacy and compliance
compliance.title: Student privacy and compliance: COPPA, FERPA and GDPR
compliance.description: Where Oomba Academy stands on COPPA, FERPA and GDPR, what student data it keeps, who receives it, and how a school can ask about a data agreement.
compliance.lead: This page is for teachers, school leaders and IT staff who check tools against student privacy laws. It sums up what our Privacy Policy says and what Oomba Academy does today. If anything here differs from the Privacy Policy, the Privacy Policy is the one that counts.

glance.li1: Students never need an email address, and we never ask for their age or home address.
glance.li1google: Students never type an email address, and we never ask for their age or home address. If your school uses Sign in with Google, we keep each student’s school Google email only to recognize their account.
glance.li2: No ads, no advertising or tracking cookies, and we never sell anyone’s personal information.
glance.li3: School accounts are made and owned by the school. We use student information only to provide Oomba Academy to the school, never for advertising.
glance.li4: A student’s real name, if the school adds one, is seen only by the school’s staff and our team.
glance.li5: Games run in a locked sandbox: no network, no cookies and no access to the rest of the site.

coppa.p1: Oomba Academy is made for kids from kindergarten to grade 8, so many of them are under 13. This is how their information is handled today:
coppa.li1: School accounts are made and owned by the school, and students sign in with a login card from school. For these accounts we act on the school’s behalf and under its direction.
coppa.li2: Parents of a school account ask the school to see or delete their child’s records, and the school can ask us.
coppa.li3: Parents of a child’s own account can email us to see what we keep, to delete it, or to stop us collecting more. There is no delete or download button yet, so we handle these requests by hand, and we check that you are the parent first.
coppa.li4: Paying for a plan is never how we ask a parent for permission.
coppa.p2: Questions about how consent works for your school’s accounts: email {email}.

ferpa.li1: Beyond what any account keeps, a school account keeps the student’s real name as the school typed it, their classes, lesson progress, written answers and their teacher’s feedback.
ferpa.li2: A student’s real name is seen only by the school’s staff and our team.
ferpa.li3: We use student information only to provide Oomba Academy to the school, never for advertising, and we don’t sell it.
ferpa.li4: Parents ask the school to see or delete records, and the school can ask us. A data agreement the school has signed with us comes first.
ferpa.p: To discuss FERPA terms for your school or district: email {email}.

gdpr.h: GDPR and UK GDPR (Europe and the UK)
gdpr.p1: Oomba Academy is in {count} languages, and schools outside the US can use it. The same rules apply everywhere: no ads, no tracking cookies, no student emails, and student information used only to provide Oomba Academy.
gdpr.p2: Schools in the European Union or the United Kingdom: please email {email} before you roll Oomba Academy out, so we can answer your questions about the GDPR or the UK GDPR first.

dpa.p1: Our Privacy Policy says that a data agreement a school has signed with us comes first.
dpa.p2: To ask about a data agreement for your school or district, including a state student privacy agreement, email {email}.

keep.li1: We keep an account’s data for as long as the account exists. None of it is deleted on a timer yet.
keep.li2: A game a student deletes is taken off the site for everyone, but a copy stays on our server.
keep.li3: There is no button yet to delete an account or download its data. For a school account, the school asks us.

others.li1: Anthropic (Claude, the AI that makes games): a student’s Builder messages, pictures and files, to make the game and to check it is safe, without the student’s name or username. Chats between friends and lesson answers are never sent to the AI.
others.li2: Google, only if your school uses Sign in with Google or a teacher connects Google Classroom. Classroom reads class names and the linked class’s students’ Google ids and names. We send only what the teacher posts, such as a lesson link with its title and due date, and each student’s lesson score out of 100: never students’ names, answers, feedback or games.
others.li3: AI voices and speech to text, where they are switched on: our Privacy Policy says exactly what each one gets.

security.li1: Passwords are stored scrambled, so we can’t read them.
security.li2: Every version of every game is checked by our safety scanner the moment it is made, and a game that tries to reach the internet or read cookies can’t be shared.
security.li3: A teacher’s Google Classroom connection is stored encrypted until they disconnect, and disconnecting also revokes it at Google.

contact.p: Email {email}. For records of a school account, the school contacts us. See also our Privacy Policy and how we keep kids safe.

teachersLive.lead: Put the game on the board. Students join on their own devices with a 7-digit code and race through your questions, on any subject, at any level. Free, with no ads, and nothing for students to type but the code.

demo.note: A one-minute video with music and captions on screen: a teacher starts a Quest Race in Science, students join on their phones with a code and race through the questions, then a child describes a game to the Builder, which makes it and plays it to check it works, and the child plays it. Last, a few of the learning games.

cta.join: Joining a game? Type the code here

how.h: From questions to a podium in a few minutes
how.lead: Real screens from a live game in a demo school with made-up names.

s1.h: Pick a game and your questions
s1.p: Choose Quest Race, Question Battle or Brain Board, then the questions: the question bank by subject and age (6 to 14), your own set, one a colleague shared, or the questions from one of your lessons.
s1.alt: The first step of hosting a live game, “What do you want to play?”: Quest Race, Question Battle and Brain Board, each with how many players it suits.

s2.h: Show the code on the board
s2.p: Students go to the join page on their device and type the 7-digit code, or scan the QR code. Their names appear as they join.
s2.alt: The projector screen before the game starts: a cartoon character the whole class plays against, a big 7-digit code, a QR code and how many players have joined.

s3.p: No app and no sign-up for an open room. In a class room, your signed-in students join with their own accounts.
s3.alt: A student's phone on the join page, with the 7-digit code typed in.

s4.p: The question is on the board and the answer buttons are on every device. Right answers score more the faster they come.
s4.alt: A student’s phone during a question: the cartoon character the class plays against at the top, then the question and four answer buttons.

s5.p: A leaderboard after each question, and at the end a results page by question and by student.
s5.alt: The projector screen showing the leaderboard with the students' scores.

race.p: A 3D island race. Every right answer gives gems and a boost, and the whole class watches the runners on the board.

battle.p: The classic: the question on the big screen, answers on every device, and a leaderboard after each one.

board.p: A board of categories on the screen. Pick a tile (or let the fastest right answer pick), and its question opens on every device. Harder tiles are worth more, and a hidden Lucky Star doubles the points.

wyr.p: The class votes on fun dilemmas and sees how it splits, and how everyone on Oomba chose. No right answers and no points: a ready-made conversation starter.

doodle.p: One player draws while the others guess, typed or out loud (or with letter tiles for younger players): spelling and vocabulary in 13 languages. Best for small groups (up to 16); you can clear a drawing or skip a turn at any time.

tug.p: Two teams pull a rope with right answers. Pick a grade from 1 to 8; every player answers their own questions on a keypad, and uneven teams pull fairly.

atlas.p: Everyone taps the country on their own world map: find it, its flag, its capital or what it is famous for. The big screen shows where the whole class tapped, and close guesses still score.

tools.li1: Teams of 2 to 6, balanced for you, with team colors and scores.
tools.li2: "Eyes on me" pauses every screen, and quick messages like "One minute left".
tools.li3: A timer of 10, 20 or 30 seconds a question, and skip or pause any time.
tools.li4: Bonus points for teamwork, kindness and effort.
tools.li5: Extra time for students who need it.
tools.li6: A co-host can run the game with you.
tools.li7: Results by question and by student. Class games are saved and download as a spreadsheet.

safe.h: Built for kids from the start
safe.li1: Students can't type anything but the code: no chat, no free-text names, no comments.
safe.li2: In an open room everyone gets a kind made-up nickname, like Brave Otter, never a real name.
safe.li3: A class room is for your own signed-in students only, and their scores go into your gradebook.
safe.li4: Codes end when the game ends, and students can report anything to you with one tap.
safe.link: Read more on our safety page.

more.p: Oomba Live is part of Oomba Academy, where students also play learning games and build their own games with a safe AI helper. One free account for your whole class.

start.h: Ready for your first live game?
start.p: Make a free grown-up account, or sign in with your school account. Pick a starter set and you can be playing in two minutes.
start.signedIn: You're signed in. Pick a game and open your room.
start.kid: Live games are hosted by teachers and other grown-ups. Ask your teacher for the code, then join here:
start.pSchool: Sign in with your school account, or get a free school account for your class. Pick a starter set and you can be playing in two minutes.

faq.h: Questions teachers ask about Oomba Live
faq.a1: Yes. Hosting live games, the starter question sets, your own sets and the results are all free, with no ads.
faq.q2: Do my students need accounts?
faq.a2: Not for an open room: students type the code and get a made-up nickname. In a class room, they use the school accounts you made for them, and their scores go into your gradebook.
faq.a3: Up to {max} in a class room. A room open to anyone with the code takes up to {open} players when a parent or other grown-up hosts it, and up to {max} when a teacher does.
faq.q4: Can I use my own questions?
faq.a4: Yes, on any subject and at any level. Write a set of up to {items} questions with 2 to 4 answers each, paste one from a spreadsheet, let AI draft one for you to edit, or turn the questions from one of your lessons into a live quiz.
faq.a5: Any device with an up-to-date browser: Chromebooks, tablets, laptops or phones. Nothing to install. You show the game on the board from your own computer.

own.p: Write quizzes for any subject and any age, from early reading to high-school chemistry.
own.li1: Type questions with 2 to 4 answers, or true or false, and a time from 5 seconds to 2 minutes each.
own.li2: Paste a whole quiz from a spreadsheet or a document in one go.
own.li3: Describe a topic and a grade, and AI drafts the questions for you to check and edit.
own.li4: Up to 100 questions in a set. Share sets with teachers at your school, or copy theirs and make them your own.
own.li5: Want a different kind of game? Build your own quiz game with the AI Builder, and it plays live with any of your question sets.

cs.title: CS Quest
cs.sub: Computer science in four games · grades 3–8
cs.about: Code a robot, solve mysteries with data, send messages across a town, and open up the machines we use every day. Each step is a short lesson, a quick check and then a game module.
cs.teachers: Every game has lesson plans you can teach in a 45-minute class, with live warm-ups, exit tickets and a standards view for your class.

cd.title: Cyber Defenders
cd.about: Join Pim the owl at the Netville post office and learn to keep messages — and each other — safe: how messages travel, passphrases and secret codes, what stays private, and how to spot a trick. Each step is a short lesson, a quick check and then a game module.
cd.teachers: Every step is mapped to the CYBER.ORG K-12 Cybersecurity Learning Standards and Common Sense Education's digital citizenship topics, with a teacher note for every unit.

nq.title: Number Quest
nq.sub: Math through the Numberworks · grades K–8
nq.about: Walk the Numberworks in the town of Netville with Tally the cat. The Launchpad gardens, for kindergarten to grade 2, grow counting, adding and taking away, tens and ones, shapes and measuring. The Explorer street, for grades 3 to 5, goes on to big numbers, groups and shares, fractions at the Bakery, then measures, shapes, charts and chance. The Pro towers, for grades 6 to 8, take on ratios, negative numbers, equations, slope, geometry and data. Each step is a short lesson, a quick check and then a game mission, and finishing earns Tally Marks and mastery laps.
nq.teachers: Every step of Launchpad Units 1–7 and the Garden Gate finale (grades K–2), of Explorer Units 1–7 and the Vault of Measures finale (grades 3–5), and of Pro Units 1–7 and the Great Clock finale (grades 6–8), is mapped to the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSS-M), with the Mathematical Practice each step spotlights and a teacher note for every unit.

why.h: Fun is the delivery system. Learning is the point.
why.lead: Good learning games lean on a few well-studied ideas from the science of learning.

b1.p: Answering to win pulls knowledge back out of memory, and recalling something is one of the most reliable ways to make it stick.

b2.p: Every answer gets a response in the moment, so mistakes are fixed while the thinking is still fresh.

b3.p: “One more round” feels like play, not a worksheet, so students practice more, without the weight of a grade.

b4.p: A game gives every student a turn, including the ones who rarely raise a hand.

b5.p: To build a game about a topic, students have to understand it well enough to teach it to a computer.

legend.sources: Covered by: the assigned lessons tagged with the standard (or with a step or a Learn game that practices it), live games that asked about it (Tug of Math Live at its grade, question sets whose questions carry the code) and the courses your students are in.
legend.practiced: Practiced: students who finished an activity that practices the standard. It means they did it, not mastery.
legend.checked: Questions: right answers out of answered questions about the standard (lesson quizzes, live games, Number Quest checks).
legend.rubric: Rubric: rubric scores on the standard, as a share of the top score. Shown once rubrics are tagged with Common Core standards.
legend.meets: Meets: a student meets a standard with at least 80% right over 3 or more questions, or a rubric score of at least two thirds. The class meets it when 80% of its students do.
legend.needs: Needs a look: students who answered 2 or more questions about the standard and got none right. Only teachers see this.
legend.games: Games with levels for several grades (Sum Racer, Fraction Factory, Word Trail, Tug of Math) count as practice only for the lesson's grade, or for the level the step is locked to. For a lesson with no grade they show under Covered by only.
legend.live: Live games such as Tug of Math Live don't record which question was about which standard, so a student's answers are shared out across the game's standards. Those numbers are estimates.
legend.courses: Number Quest counts work done with a school account, or since the student joined this class. One check (3 questions) alone is not enough to meet a standard.

help.late: Work still missing after the due date. "Done late" means it was finished after the due date.
help.names: The grey name under a student's name is the one they have in games and on the class screen.

email.step1: Add your teachers on the People tab, by their real names. Each one gets a school account and a login card to print or pass on.
email.step2: Make your classes and give each one its teacher.
email.step3: Add your students: paste their names, one per line. Each one gets a printable login card.
email.step4: Check your school's rules on the Settings tab. Chat between students is off unless you turn it on.
email.teachersText: Teachers sign in and land on their Classroom page. The quickest first win is a live game: tap "Host a live game", put the code on the board, and the class joins from any device. They can also turn a lesson they already teach into a quiz with "Turn a lesson into a game".

email.help: Questions? Just reply to this email. A real person answers, usually within one school day.
email.changeLater: You can change your username and your name later on your Me page.

start.heading: How do you want to start?

start.directText: Go straight to the Builder and describe your game in your own words.

else.title: Something else

worlds.wild-woods: A sunny forest with a river, cliffs and a camp.

worlds.under-the-sea: A coral reef to swim through as a dolphin, a turtle or a fish.

kind.heading: What are you making?

classgame.text: For the whole room, on the board: Category Board, bingo, flashcards, a quiet game, a spinner, a scoreboard.

arcade.title: Arcade game
arcade.text: A fun game to play and share: run, catch, quiz, race, in 2D or a 3D world.

practise.heading: What should students practice?
practise.text: Type a topic. The Builder makes 5 problems with steps and hints.
practise.label: What should students practice?
practise.placeholder: For example: equivalent fractions with eighths and sixths
practise.privacy: The Builder gets your topic, the class's grade and what you add about your lesson. Never students' names or work.

help.heading: How much help?
help.hint: Pick one or more. With more than one, students can switch between them.

watch.title: Watch
watch.text: Shows how each one is done, then students try.

count.title: Count up
count.text: Step answers with ▲ ▼ buttons, no typing.

guided.title: Guided
guided.text: Steps open, with up to 3 hints.

own.title: On my own

use.heading: How will students use it?
use.note: You can always show it on the board from the Teacher button, and a fresh set of questions is made whenever possible.

screen.title: On their devices
screen.text: Each student works on their own copy, with steps and hints. Results go to Progress.

worksheet.title: On paper
worksheet.text: A printable worksheet with an answer key.

lesson.heading: Your lesson
lesson.hint: Optional. Add a lesson plan or say what you want, and the Builder fits the activity to your lesson.
lesson.safe: Don't include student names or work. We remove any we find.
lesson.fileTitle: Add a lesson plan or worksheet
lesson.fileText: PDF, Word (.docx), text or Markdown, up to 5 MB and 10 pages. From Google Docs: File, Download, then .docx or .pdf.
lesson.describeHelp: Tap a prompt to add a heading, then write under it.

prompt.goal: What should students be able to do by the end?

lesson.placeholder: For example: add fractions with the same denominator. Many students add the denominators too.

top.editHint: Drag to move · drag a corner to resize · or use the arrow keys

tray.heading: From your teacher today

eyes.title: Eyes up front

bg.heading: Background

text.name: Text and agenda

ican.name: I can… objective

ican.empty: Add today's goal in Edit screen.

timer.desc: Count down or count up, with big digits.
timer.editBad: Type minutes (8) or minutes and seconds (8:30), up to 180 minutes.

schedule.name: Schedule for the day
schedule.desc: Today's periods, with the one on now lit up. Set a standard week, upload an agenda or connect a calendar.
schedule.empty: Add today's periods in Edit screen.
schedule.after: That's the end of today's schedule.
schedule.uploadHint: A calendar file (.ics) fills the week ahead. A .csv or .txt file, or pasted text, takes one line a period, like “8:30–9:15 Reading”; a line with a day's name (Monday) starts that day.
schedule.imported: {n, plural, one {# period added.} other {# periods added.}}
schedule.importNone: No times found. Try one line a period, like “8:30–9:15 Reading”, or a calendar file (.ics).
schedule.calNote: Google Calendar: Settings → your calendar → “Secret address in iCal format”. Outlook: Settings → Calendar → Shared calendars → Publish → ICS link. Today's timed events become the schedule, and everyone who sees this widget sees them, so connect a calendar meant for the class. The address itself stays private.
schedule.calToday: Today's events come from this calendar (checked every 15 minutes). On a day with none, the schedule below is shown.

weather.name: Weather
weather.desc: Today's weather in your school's town.
weather.empty: Pick your town in Edit screen.
weather.clear: Sunny and clear. A great day!
weather.drizzle: A little drizzle. Bring a coat.
weather.storm: Stormy. Stay inside if you can.

qr.desc: Put a link on screen for tablets to scan.
qr.empty: Pick what the code opens in Edit screen.
qr.gone: That link isn't available any more. Pick another in Edit screen.
qr.tooLong: This address is too long for a QR code — try a shorter link.

s.norepeat: Don't repeat until everyone's had a turn

picker.awayNote: Ticked students aren't picked today. This resets tomorrow.
picker.noItems: Type some items in Edit screen.

noise.name: Voice meter
noise.desc: How loud is the room? Uses your mic; nothing is recorded.
noise.note: Sound stays on this computer. Nothing is recorded, saved or sent.
noise.denied: The mic is blocked. Allow it in the browser to use the meter.

help.name: Help queue
help.desc: Students tap "I need help" or "I'm done".
help.doneMine: Your teacher can see you're done.
help.hidden: Names are hidden on the projector.

check.name: Quick check

check.empty: Send a quick check to see how everyone's doing.
check.question: Question (you can leave it out)

tiles.name: Oomba tiles
tiles.desc: Games and lessons to open with one tap.
tiles.empty: Pick games and lessons in Edit screen.

countdown.name: Countdown to a day
countdown.desc: Days and hours until field trips, shows or holidays: one or several on one card.
countdown.empty: Pick the day in Edit screen.
countdown.past: That day has come and gone.
countdown.label: What's coming
countdown.full: A card holds up to {n} countdowns.

calendar.name: Calendar
calendar.desc: Today's date, the month, and days you mark.
calendar.label: Label

symbols.name: Work symbols
symbols.desc: How to work right now: silent, whisper, partner, together, hand up.

light.name: Traffic light
light.desc: Red, yellow or green, with your own words for each.

dice.name: Dice
dice.desc: Roll 1 to 6 dice and see the total.

random.name: Random number
random.desc: A number between a smallest and a biggest.

groups.name: Group maker
groups.desc: Random groups from the class, by Oomba name.
groups.none: No students to put in groups.
groups.note: Students marked away in the picker are left out.

score.name: Scoreboard
score.desc: Team points with plus and minus buttons.
score.undone: The last point was taken back.
score.resetConfirm: Set every student's points back to zero?
score.hidden: Each student's points are hidden on the projector.
score.nobody: No students in this class yet.
score.pick: Pick what it's for. Points are only ever given, never taken away.
score.classGiven: The whole class earned a point for {reason}
score.classPick: A point for the whole class
score.gcPostHint: A whole-class point goes to the class stream. A student's point goes only to that student. Never names or rankings.
score.gcFailed: Couldn't post to Google Classroom just now. The point is saved.
score.gcNotOnClassroom: Not posted: this student isn't linked to Google Classroom. The point is saved.
score.gcTooMany: Google Classroom posts are paused for a while (10 an hour). The point is saved.
score.gcReconnect: Google Classroom needs connecting again to post. The point is saved.
score.gcOn: Points will also go to Google Classroom.
score.onlyYou: Only you and your teacher see your points.

fractions.name: Fractions
fractions.desc: Compare, add, subtract, multiply and divide with bars and circles, and see one number as a fraction, decimal and percent.
fractions.tooSmall: These pieces would be too tiny to see, so they are not drawn.
fractions.samePrompt: Press Same-size pieces to see why.
fractions.howto: Tap a bar to shade parts. Use − and + to change the pieces.
fractions.howtoOp: Change each number with − and +. Type your answer, then Check.
fractions.howtoMul: Use − and + on each number. The overlap is the answer.
fractions.helpUse:
Choose Compare, Add, Subtract, Multiply or Divide.
Type your answer and press Check. Next step gives a hint.
Show the answer when everyone has had a go.
fractions.helpIdeas: Show 5/10 ÷ 2/9 and press Fit one more together: how many fit?
fractions.below: {b} is bigger than {a}, so the answer is less than zero.
fractions.think: Work it out, then show the answer.
fractions.howtoDiv: How many of the second fit in the first? Press Fit one more.
fractions.noZero: Nothing can be divided by zero, so the second numerator stays at 1 or more.
fractions.checkSimplify: Close: that is the same amount. Is it simplified?
fractions.checkNo: Not yet. Try again, or press Next step.
fractions.checkUnread: Type a fraction like 3/4 or a mixed number like 2 1/4.
fractions.stepGrid: Cut a square {c} by {r}: {n} small parts
fractions.stepShade: Shade {a} along the bottom and {b} up the side
fractions.howtoEq: The first two bars are the question. Shade the last bar to show the answer.
fractions.eqHint: Change the parts with − and +, then tap parts to shade them. Add a whole if the answer is more than one.
fractions.limitWholes: That's as big as it goes. Each fraction can be at most 3 wholes, and {f} is already 3 wholes.
fractions.limitTop: That's as big as it goes. The top number can be at most 12.
fractions.limitBottom: That's as big as it goes. The bottom number can be at most 12.

numline.name: Number line
numline.desc: Whole numbers, fractions, decimals and negatives. Tap to place points, drag to jump. Grades K–8.
numline.jumpFrom: Jump from {v}: now pick where it lands
numline.hint: Tap the line to place a point, or drag along it to jump.
numline.range: Up to 240 steps fit on one line.
numline.howto: Point: tap the line. Jump: drag from one number to another.
numline.helpUse:
Tap a point again to take it away.
Arrow keys move the marker; Enter places a point or a jump.
Options: the range, and whole numbers, fractions or decimals.
numline.helpIdeas: Jump 3/4 three times from 0. Where do you land?

coord.name: Coordinate plane
coord.desc: Plot points and draw y = mx + b. Change the slope and start, with a table of values. Grades 5–8.
coord.hint: Arrow keys move, Enter plots a point.
coord.noLine: Tap the grid to plot points.
coord.howto: Tap the grid to plot a point. Use − and + to change the line.
coord.helpUse:
Tap a point again to take it away.
Slope changes the steepness; Starts at moves the line up or down.
The table gives exact values. Options: one quadrant or four.
coord.helpIdeas: Plot three points from the table and ask for the rule.

graph.name: Graph maker
graph.desc: Bar, line, picture and dot plots from your own numbers or a quick check's totals.
graph.title: Title
graph.label: Label
graph.counts: Only the totals come over, never who answered what.
graph.howto: Pick a kind of graph. Put your own numbers in Options.
graph.helpUse:
Bar, line, picture and dot graphs show the same numbers.
Options: a title, and up to 12 labels and numbers.
Teachers can graph a quick check's totals from Options.
graph.helpIdeas: Ask a quick check about favorite fruit, then graph its totals.

base10.name: Base-ten blocks
base10.desc: Ones, tens and hundreds. Drag them in, trade 10 for 1 and back. Grades K–4.
base10.hint: 10 of a kind can be traded for 1 of the next.
base10.howto: Tap or drag blocks onto the mats. Trade 10 for 1 of the next.
base10.helpUse:
− and + under a mat take away or add one block.
Drag a block off a mat to take it away.
Trading changes the blocks, never the number.
base10.helpIdeas: Build 205, then trade to get ready to take away 30.

placeval.name: Place value
placeval.desc: Base-ten blocks and a place value chart: trade tens for ones, and read numbers from millions to thousandths.
placeval.howto: Tap a column, then use − and + to change its digit.
placeval.helpUse:
− and + carry and borrow across the places.
Times 10 and Divide by 10 move every digit one place.
Options: digit discs, and places after the decimal point.
placeval.helpIdeas: Show 3405, press Times 10: what moved, and what stayed?

tenframe.name: Ten frames
tenframe.desc: One or two ten frames with red and yellow counters and number bonds. Grades K–2.
tenframe.howto: Tap a box for a red counter, again for yellow, again to empty it.
tenframe.helpUse:
Red + and Yellow + fill the next box; Take one empties the last.
The number bond shows how many more make ten.
Options: two frames, swap the colors, fill with red.
tenframe.helpIdeas: Show 7 for two seconds, hide the screen, and ask how many.

hundreds.name: Number chart
hundreds.desc: A 1–100, 0–99 or 1–120 chart. Shade numbers, skip count and hide numbers to guess.
hundreds.howto: Tap numbers to shade them. Pick a skip count to see a pattern.
hundreds.helpUse:
Tap a shaded number again to unshade it.
Hide numbers hides the shaded ones, or all, to guess.
Options: 1-100 or 0-99. Clear takes it all away.
hundreds.helpIdeas: Count by 9: what pattern do the digits make?

area.name: Multiply and divide
area.desc: Area models and arrays with partial products, and a times table grid up to 12 × 12. Bar models too: groups, parts and comparing.
area.hint: Split a side to break the product into easier parts.
area.howto: Use − and + for rows and columns. Split a side to break it up.
area.helpUse:
Array shows dots in rows; Area model shows a rectangle.
Split by place value shows each partial product.
Options: choose exactly where each side is split.
area.helpIdeas: Show 14 × 6 as 10 × 6 and 4 × 6, and add the parts.

times.name: Times table grid
times.desc: Up to 12 × 12. Light up a fact, a row, a column or the square numbers.
times.pick: Tap a box to light up a fact.
times.howto: Tap a box to light up a fact. Pick what else to show.
times.helpUse:
The menu lights a row, a column, squares or turn-around facts.
Hide answers blanks every product, so the class can guess.
Arrow keys and Enter work too. Options: 10 × 10 or 12 × 12.
times.helpIdeas: Light up the 9 row: what pattern do the digits make?

tclock.name: Teaching clock
tclock.desc: Hands that move together, a digital readout and elapsed time.
tclock.hint: Drag a hand, or use the arrow keys.
tclock.howto: Drag a hand to change the time. The other hand follows.
tclock.helpUse:
The buttons move 5 minutes or 1 hour back or on.
Options: the digital time and 24-hour time.
Elapsed time, in Options, shows how long from start to end.
tclock.helpIdeas: Turn the digital time off and ask the class to read the clock.

fdp.name: Fraction, decimal, percent
fdp.desc: One number three ways, side by side, with a 10 × 10 grid.
fdp.howto: Use − and + on the numerator and denominator, or tap the grid.
fdp.helpUse:
The cards show it as a fraction, a decimal and a percent.
A decimal that repeats ends in …
Tap the 10 × 10 grid to shade hundredths; arrow keys work too.
fdp.helpIdeas: Ask for 3/8 as a decimal, then set it here to check.

board.name: Whiteboard
board.desc: Draw and write on the projector. Never saved or sent anywhere.
board.note: Drawings stay on this screen only and are gone when the page reloads.
board.keys: Arrow keys move the pen; Space puts it down or lifts it.

picture.name: Picture

geoboard.name: Shape board
geoboard.desc: Make shapes with bands on a grid, dots or a circle, with exact area and perimeter. Make and measure angles with a protractor.
